items.name: GDPR lawful basis and consent for marketing (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Articles 6, 7 and 21)
items.one_line: Marketing to people in the EU needs a lawful basis (consent or legitimate interests), consent must be separate, plain-language and as easy to withdraw as to give, and an objection to direct marketing ends it absolutely.
aliases: right to object to direct marketing

sources.title: gdpr-info.eu: Art. 6 GDPR Lawfulness of processing
sources.supports: Art 6(1)(a) consent for specific purposes; Art 6(1)(f) legitimate interests

sources.title: gdpr-info.eu: Art. 7 GDPR Conditions for consent
sources.supports: consent request clearly distinguishable, plain language, withdrawal as easy as giving, no bundling with a contract

sources.title: gdpr-info.eu: Art. 21 GDPR Right to object
sources.supports: absolute right to object to direct marketing, to be flagged at the first communication

items.note: In force (Regulation (EU) 2016/679, text read on gdpr-info.eu, an unofficial but verbatim reprint, 2026-10-04). Rules for marketing copy aimed at EU residents: (1) processing is lawful on consent only when given 'for one or more specific purposes' (Art 6(1)(a)); otherwise the brand must rely on legitimate interests, which fail where 'overridden by the interests or fundamental rights' of the person, 'in particular where the data subject is a child' (Art 6(1)(f)). (2) A consent request inside a form that covers other things must be 'clearly distinguishable from the other matters', in 'clear and plain language' (Art 7(2)): separate, unticked marketing opt-in, never buried in terms. (3) 'It shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent' (Art 7(3)): every email or message carries a one-click opt-out. (4) Do not make a service or download conditional on marketing consent that the service does not need (Art 7(4)). (5) Objection to direct marketing is absolute: 'the personal data shall no longer be processed for such purposes', and the right must be 'explicitly brought to the attention' of the person at the first communication, 'clearly and separately' (Art 21(2)-(4)). Email and SMS marketing also need ePrivacy consent rules (national laws implementing Directive 2002/58/EC Art 13; UK: comp:uk_pecr).

items.name: US TCPA rules for marketing calls and texts (47 CFR 64.1200)
items.one_line: US autodialled or prerecorded marketing calls and texts to mobiles need the recipient's prior express written consent, telephone solicitations must respect the national Do-Not-Call registry and 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time, and any reasonable opt-out such as replying STOP must be honoured.

sources.title: eCFR: 47 CFR 64.1200 Delivery restrictions
sources.supports: current text: (a)(2) written consent for telemarketing robocalls/robotexts, (a)(10) revocation, (c) calling hours and national do-not-call, (f) definitions

items.note: Current eCFR text (fetched 2026-10-04 by the first compliance worker into work/compliance/txt/tcpa_cfr.txt and re-read here); the FCC has phased in and delayed parts of its 2024 consent-revocation order, so check the eCFR 'effective' notes before quoting a date (not confirmed here). Rules: (1) no call or text 'that includes or introduces an advertisement or constitutes telemarketing' using an autodialer or artificial/prerecorded voice to a mobile without 'prior express written consent' (64.1200(a)(2)); texts are treated as calls (the section refers to 'text message, including a short message service (SMS) call'). (2) Prior express written consent = a signed written agreement (e-signature allowed) that clearly authorises the seller to send telemarketing to a named number, with a 'clear and conspicuous disclosure' (64.1200(f)): the opt-in checkbox copy is legal text, write it plainly and never make it a condition of purchase. (3) Revocation: replies such as 'stop', 'quit', 'end', 'revoke', 'opt out', 'cancel' or 'unsubscribe' are per se valid, any reasonable method counts, and requests must be honoured 'within a reasonable time not to exceed ten business days' (64.1200(a)(10)). (4) No telephone solicitation before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. at the recipient's location, or to numbers on the national do-not-call registry (64.1200(c)). For India SMS see comp:trai_tcccpr_2018; EU/UK see comp:gdpr_marketing_consent and comp:uk_pecr.

items.name: Reserve Bank of India (Digital Lending) Directions, 2025
items.one_line: Loan apps and their lending service providers must show every matching loan offer with lender name, APR and repayment side by side, without dark patterns that push one lender, and must take explicit, purpose-stated consent before collecting data.

sources.title: RBI notification RBI/2025-26/36, DOR.STR.REC.19/21.07.001/2025-26 dated 8 May 2025: Reserve Bank of India (Digital Lending) Directions, 2025
sources.supports: commencement (para 2), multi-lender display and dark-pattern ban (para 6), disclosures and KFS (para 8), consent for data (para 12)

items.note: Issued 8 May 2025; in force immediately except para 6 (multi-lender display) from 1 Nov 2025 and para 17 (DLA directory) from 15 Jun 2025 (para 2, RBI page read 2026-10-04). They consolidate the 2 Sep 2022 digital lending guidelines; whether RBI has since folded them into a later consolidated master direction was not checked. Rules for fintech, loan-app and finfluencer copy: (1) where a lending service provider works with several lenders, the content it displays 'shall be unbiased, objective and shall not directly/ indirectly promote or push a product of a particular RE, including the use of dark patterns/deceptive patterns' (para 6(iv)); ranking is allowed only on a 'publicly pre-disclosed metric'. (2) The loan-offer view must name the lender and show amount, tenor, APR, monthly repayment and penal charges 'in a way which enables the borrower to make a fair comparison' (para 6(iii)): never advertise a loan without the lender's name, and quote APR, not a teaser 'flat' rate. (3) Borrower gets a Key Fact Statement and a cooling-off exit 'not being less than one day' (paras 8, 10). (4) Data collection only 'with prior and explicit consent', purpose 'disclosed at each stage' (para 12): no contact-list or gallery access CTAs. Dark patterns are defined by reference to comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023.

items.name: UK Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 Schedule 20: commercial practices always considered unfair (incl. fake reviews)
items.one_line: UK blacklist of 32 practices that are unfair in all circumstances, several of them pure copy problems: fake or secretly incentivised reviews, unlabelled paid editorial, false 'limited time' claims, false cure claims, misleading 'free', posing as a consumer and direct appeals to children.

sources.title: legislation.gov.uk: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, Schedule 20 (latest available revised text)
sources.supports: full text of paragraphs 1-32 and commencement notes (in force 6.4.2025 by S.I. 2025/272)

items.note: In force 6 April 2025 for every paragraph read (commencement notes on legislation.gov.uk, read in a browser 2026-10-04; python fetch got an empty bot-check response). Rules a copywriter must remember: (1) para 13: never write, submit or commission 'a fake consumer review' (one that 'purports to be, but is not, based on a person's genuine experience') or a review 'that conceals the fact it has been incentivised'; publishing reviews 'in a misleading way' includes hiding negatives or giving positives greater prominence. AI-written reviews count ('writing' includes creating by any means). (2) para 12: paid promotion inside editorial content must be made clear 'in the content or by images or sounds clearly identifiable by the consumer' (advertorials, sponsored articles). (3) para 7: no false 'only available for a limited time' claims made 'to elicit an immediate decision'. (4) para 19: no false claims that a product can 'prevent or treat disease', restore a physiological function or 'modify a person's appearance'. (5) para 23: 'free', 'gratis', 'without charge' only if the consumer pays nothing beyond the unavoidable cost of responding and delivery. Also: para 25 no posing as a consumer (fake grassroots posts), para 30 no 'direct appeal to children to buy' or to pester parents, para 3 no unauthorised trust marks, para 14 no fear claims about safety. Ad-rule companion: comp:uk_cap_code.

items.name: Meta Advertising Standards (Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, WhatsApp ads): personal attributes and health claims
items.one_line: Meta ad copy must not assert or imply a viewer's personal attributes ('Are you diabetic?', 'Meet other seniors'), must not attack appearance or promise cures or timed results for weight-loss, cosmetic and health products, and must follow local law and self-regulatory codes.

sources.title: Meta Transparency Center: Introduction to the Advertising Standards
sources.supports: principles, review process, advertiser responsibility for local law and self-regulatory codes

sources.title: Meta Transparency Center: Privacy Violations and Personal Attributes (change log latest Jun 27, 2024)
sources.supports: ban on asserting or implying personal attributes, with allowed and disallowed copy examples

sources.title: Meta Transparency Center: Health and Wellness (change log latest Jul 22, 2026)
sources.supports: 18+ targeting for weight-loss/cosmetic ads, no inferiority statements, no cure claims for listed diseases, no clickbait timed outcomes

items.note: Pages read in a browser 2026-10-04 (python fetch is refused with HTTP 400). Rules: (1) personal attributes: ads 'must not contain content that asserts or implies personal attributes', including race, religion, age, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability, physical or mental health, 'vulnerable financial status', voting status, criminal record or name; Meta's own examples allow 'Depression counseling' but reject 'Depression getting you down? Get help now.' and 'Are you bankrupt? Check out our services.' Write about the product, not about the reader's condition; 'you/your' is fine only without an attribute. (2) Health and wellness: weight-loss, diet and cosmetic ads must target 18+ and may not contain 'statements of inferiority about physical appearance'. (3) No claims 'to cure, heal, or eliminate' an exhaustive list of conditions (Diabetes, Herpes, Thyroid, Psoriasis, Ebola, Cancer, Autism, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ALS, HIV); symptom-management claims are outside this rule. (4) No clickbait 'sensational language with exaggerated or extreme claims, or promises of specific outcomes within a set timeframe without disclaimers or qualifiers'. (5) Advertisers must also comply with 'all local laws, regulations and, where applicable, self-regulatory advertising codes' (intro page): in India that means comp:asci_code, comp:dmr_act_1954 and comp:fssai_advertising_claims_2018 on top. Branded content and political ads: comp:meta_branded_content, comp:meta_siep_ads.

items.name: Meta policy on ads about social issues, elections or politics (authorisation and 'Paid for by' disclaimer, incl. India)
items.one_line: Anyone running a Meta ad by or about a candidate, party, election or social issue must complete Meta's authorisation, carry a verified 'Paid for by' disclaimer, disclose realistic AI-made or AI-edited media, and in India must not discourage voting or question an election's legitimacy.

sources.title: Meta Transparency Center: Ads about Social Issues, Elections or Politics (change log latest Jul 1, 2026)
sources.supports: authorisation requirement, Paid for by disclaimer, AI disclosure, automated AI detection from 1 Jun 2026, country rules for India

items.note: Page read in a browser 2026-10-04 (latest change-log entry Jul 1, 2026). India's authorisation steps sit in the Business Help Center (facebook.com/id), not read here. Rules: (1) any advertiser 'located in or targeting people in designated countries' must complete Meta's authorization for ads made by, on behalf of or about a candidate, political figure or party, about any election, referendum or 'get out the vote' campaign, or about 'any social issue'; news publishers identified by Meta are exempt. (2) Such ads need a verified 'Paid for by' disclaimer; without it the ad is disapproved and still added to the Ad Library. (3) Advertisers 'must also disclose' photorealistic images, video or realistic audio made or edited with third-party generative AI that depict a real person saying or doing something they did not, a realistic person or event that does not exist, or a fake recording of a real event; non-disclosure means rejection and penalties for repeat failures; from June 1, 2026 Meta also auto-detects and shows an 'AI Info' label. (4) In India (with the US, Brazil, Israel, Mexico, UK) ads 'must not discourage people from voting or call into question the legitimacy of an upcoming or ongoing election, or contain premature claims of election victory'. (5) The advertiser must still comply with local disclaimer, blackout-period and spending rules: in India pair with comp:eci_mcc (MCMC pre-certification) and comp:eci_ai_content_advisory.

items.name: Copyright Act, 1957 (India) section 52: fair dealing and other acts that are not infringement
items.one_line: Indian copyright lets you use a work without permission only for listed purposes: private use and research, criticism or review, and reporting current events; criticism and review need an acknowledgment naming the work and its author, and moral rights stay with the author.

sources.title: Copyright Office, Government of India: The Copyright Act, 1957 (14 of 1957), as amended (text incl. Act 27 of 2012)
sources.supports: s.52(1)(a) fair dealing purposes, s.52(1)(m) reproduction of articles on current topics, acknowledgment proviso, s.57 author's special rights

items.note: Act in force; s.52(1)(a) substituted by Act 27 of 2012 w.e.f. 21-6-2012 (footnote in the official PDF read 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) 'a fair dealing with any work, not being a computer programme' is allowed only for '(i) private or personal use, including research; (ii) criticism or review ...; (iii) the reporting of current events and current affairs' (s.52(1)(a)). Entertainment, marketing or 'just a reaction' use is not on the list: quote only what the critique or news report needs. (2) The proviso at the end of s.52(1) makes several exceptions, including criticism or review under (a)(ii), apply only if the use is 'accompanied by an acknowledgment' identifying the work by its title and, unless anonymous, its author: credit every quoted line, clip or screenshot. (3) s.52(1)(m) allows a periodical to reproduce 'an article on current economic, political, social or religious topics' unless the author 'expressly reserved' the right. (4) s.57: independently of copyright, the author may claim authorship and restrain 'distortion, mutilation, modification' prejudicial to honour or reputation: memes and parody edits of someone's work can still be challenged. The Act does not define how much quoting is 'fair'; Indian courts decide case by case (no case law harvested here).

items.name: TRAI Telecom Commercial Communications Customer Preference Regulations, 2018 (TCCCPR, DLT) and Second Amendment Regulations, 2025
items.one_line: Every commercial SMS or call in India goes out under a registered header and a registered content template on TRAI's DLT system, promotional messages need consent or an unblocked preference, and since 2025 headers carry -P/-S/-T/-G suffixes and each promotional message must carry an opt-out.

sources.title: TRAI notification dated 19 July 2018: Telecom Commercial Communications Customer Preference Regulations, 2018 (6 of 2018)
sources.supports: definitions of header, consent template, content template; preference time bands; consent revocation duties

sources.title: TRAI notification dated 12 February 2025: TCCCPR (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2025 (1 of 2025)
sources.supports: commencement, -P/-S/-T/-G header suffixes, opt-out in every promotional message, mixed content treated as promotional, URL/APK/call-back whitelisting, template rules

sources.title: TRAI: TCCCPR page
sources.supports: links to the principal regulation and directions

items.note: Principal regulation notified 19 Jul 2018; Second Amendment notified 12 Feb 2025, in force 'after thirty days from the date of their publication in the Official Gazette', with some regulations after sixty days (reg. 1(3) of the 2025 text; gazette publication date not read here). Both PDFs read 2026-10-04. Rules for SMS and voice copy: (1) a header is 'an alphanumeric string of maximum eleven characters' registered to the sender, and every message body must match a registered content template (2018 definitions); the 2025 explanatory note adds that at least 30% of a template must stay fixed, more than three variables needs justification, and templates unused for 90 days are deactivated. (2) Headers must show the message type by suffix: '"-P", "-S", "-T", and "-G" for Promotional, Service, Transactional, and Government Messages' (2025). (3) 'the Sender shall give an opt-out mechanism to the Recipient in the same Message', and 'if promotional content is mixed with any type of Transactional or Service Message, such Message shall be treated as a Promotional Message' (2025): never slip an offer into an OTP or order update. (4) Promotional messages reach only people who have not blocked the category or who gave explicit digital consent via a registered consent template that 'clearly mentions purpose of the consent and details of sender' (2018 definition; 2025 text). (5) Links, APKs, OTT links and call-back numbers in messages must be whitelisted by the sender (2025). WhatsApp Business messaging is governed by Meta's policies, not by DLT (not harvested here).

items.name: Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018 (FSSAI)
items.one_line: Food and beverage ads and labels in India: claims must be truthful and scientifically substantiated, words like natural, fresh, pure, original, traditional and authentic have legal conditions, disease-cure claims and 'recommended by doctors' lines are banned, and no ad may run down another maker's product.

sources.title: FSSAI: Compendium of Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018 (Version I, 02.03.2021)
sources.supports: regs 4 (general principles), 5-9 (nutrition and health claims, Schedule V words), 10 (prohibited claims), 11 (approval of claims)

items.note: Notified 19 Nov 2018 (No. 1-94/FSSAI/SP(Claims and Advertisements)/2017), compliance due by 1 Jul 2019; the compendium read 2026-10-04 is 'Version I (02.03.2021)', so later amendments, if any, are not reflected (not checked). Rules: (1) 'Claims must be truthful, unambiguous, meaningful, not misleading' and nutrition or health attributes must be 'scientifically substantiated by validated methods' (reg 4(1), 4(6)). (2) Do not 'encourage or condone excess consumption', suggest a balanced diet is not enough, 'undermine the importance of healthy lifestyles', or portray a food as a meal replacement unless permitted (reg 4(2), 4(3), 4(10), 4(11)). (3) 'natural', 'fresh', 'pure', 'original', 'traditional' ('existed for a generation (thirty years)'), 'authentic', 'genuine', 'real' may only be used under the conditions in the regulations; 'home-made' or 'home cooked' wording that may mislead 'shall not be used'; a misleading brand name needs the 3 mm disclaimer '*This is only a brand name or trade mark and does not represent its true nature' (reg 4(7), Schedule V). (4) No claim that a food helps 'prevention, alleviation, treatment or cure of a disease' unless specifically permitted, no 'recommended by the medical or nutrition or health professionals' wording, no fear-arousing claims about similar foods (reg 10(1), 10(2), 10(5)). (5) No ad 'that undermines the products of any other manufacturer' (reg 10(7)); claims in ads must match the label (reg 4(12)); the FSSAI logo and licence number may not be used to promote sale (reg 4(9)). Reduction-of-disease-risk claims need prior FSSAI approval (reg 11).

items.name: Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954
items.one_line: Criminal law: no one may take part in publishing an ad suggesting a drug or 'magic remedy' (talisman, mantra, kavacha) for the diseases in its Schedule, for sexual capacity, conception or miscarriage, or menstrual disorders, and no drug ad may be false or misleading.

sources.title: Indian Kanoon (secondary reproduction of statute text): The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 (Act No. 21 of 1954)
sources.supports: ss.2 (definitions: advertisement, drug, magic remedy, taking part in publication), 3, 4, 5 and 7 (penalty)

sources.title: India Code: Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954
sources.supports: official statute database entry (returned an error page and 504 timeouts to fetch and browser on 2026-10-04)

items.note: In force since 1954 (Act 21 of 1954). Official India Code page failed on 2026-10-04, so the text was read on Indian Kanoon, a secondary but verbatim reproduction (medium confidence; the Schedule of diseases was NOT in that copy: read it on India Code before naming a disease). Rules: (1) s.3: no person 'shall take any part in the publication of any advertisement referring to any drug in terms which suggest ... the use of that drug' for miscarriage or prevention of conception, 'maintenance or improvement of the capacity of human beings for sexual pleasure', correction of menstrual disorder, or 'diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment or prevention' of any disease in the Schedule. (2) s.4: no drug ad that 'gives a false impression regarding the true character of the drug', 'makes a false claim', or is 'otherwise false or misleading in any material particular'. (3) 'drug' is wide: any article other than food 'intended to affect or influence in any way the structure or any organic function of the body' (s.2(b)(iii)), so many ayurvedic, wellness and 'booster' products are covered; 'advertisement' includes labels and any announcement by light, sound or smoke (s.2(a)). (4) s.5: no ad for a 'magic remedy' (a 'talisman, mantra, kavacha, and any other charm') claiming such powers. (5) 'taking any part in the publication' includes printing it (s.2(d)), so the copywriter, influencer and publisher are exposed, not only the brand. s.7: imprisonment up to six months or fine or both on first conviction, up to one year on a subsequent conviction.

items.name: Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950: national flag, PM, President and government names in ads
items.one_line: No one may use, for any trade, business or profession, any name or emblem in the Act's Schedule (Indian national flag, Government of India or State emblems and seals, the President, 'the Prime Minister of India', Mahatma Gandhi, any name suggesting government patronage, and more) without the Central Government's permission.

sources.title: High Court of Tripura judges' library scan (EBC edition): The Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950 (Act 12 of 1950), with Rules 1982 and the Schedule
sources.supports: ss.2-3 and the Schedule items 1-11 as amended (read as page images 2026-10-04)

items.note: In force since 1950, Schedule amended by notifications up to 2011 per the footnotes (scanned publisher edition hosted by a High Court, read as images 2026-10-04: medium-high confidence; India Code copy not reachable). Rules: (1) s.3: no use 'for the purpose of any trade, business, calling or profession' of 'any name or emblem specified in the Schedule or any colourable imitation thereof' without permission. (2) Schedule includes: the Indian National Flag (item 3); the name, emblem or seal of the Government of India or any State (item 4); the President, Governor, Republic or Union of India (item 6); 'Any name which may suggest or be calculated to suggest' government patronage (item 7); Rashtrapati, Rashtrapati Bhavan, Raj Bhavan (item 9); the name or pictorial representation of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, Mahatma Gandhi, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, Smt Indira Gandhi 'or the Prime Minister of India' (item 9-A); Lal Bahadur Shastri (item 9-B); government medals and decorations (item 10); UN, WHO, UNESCO, ICAO emblems. (3) For a brand, agency or influencer: no PM photo, national flag or 'Govt. approved'/'Sarkari' style names in commercial ads or brand names. Political-party and government publicity is not 'trade, business, calling or profession'; that is governed by election law (comp:eci_mcc). For TV/cable ads see also comp:cable_tv_advertising_code (no exploiting the national emblem or a national leader).

items.name: Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994 rule 7: Advertising Code (TV and cable ads)
items.one_line: Ads carried on Indian cable TV must obey the law and the ASCI Code, must not deride any race, caste or creed, exploit the national emblem or a national leader, project women in a derogatory way, claim miraculous properties, or have religious or political objects, and are capped at twelve minutes an hour.

sources.title: Ministry of Information and Broadcasting: Programme and Advertising Codes prescribed under the Cable Television Network Rules, 1994 (Rule 6 and Rule 7), as on 02.01.2025
sources.supports: full text of rule 7 sub-rules (1)-(12)

items.note: Text as on 2 Jan 2025 (MIB PDF read 2026-10-04). Applies to TV and cable channels; digital-only ads fall under the ASCI Code and CCPA rules instead. Rules: (1) rule 7(2): no ad that '(i) derides any race, caste, colour, creed and nationality', '(v) exploits the national emblem, or any part of the Constitution or the person or personality of a national leader or a State dignitary', (vi) projects 'a derogatory image of women', (vii) exploits dowry or child marriage, or (viii) promotes tobacco, alcohol or infant milk substitutes (brand extensions only under strict conditions). (2) rule 7(3): 'No advertisement shall be permitted, the objects whereof, are wholly or mainly of a religious or political nature'; 7(3A): no references 'which hurt religious sentiments'. (3) rule 7(5): no suggestion that the product 'has some special or miraculous or super-natural property or quality, which is difficult of being proved'. (4) rule 7(9): an ad that violates the ASCI Code (comp:asci_code) 'shall not be carried'; 7(10): ads must be 'clearly distinguishable from the programme'. (5) rule 7(11): 'twelve minutes per hours', of which up to ten minutes commercial ads. Political ads on TV during elections additionally need MCMC certification (comp:eci_mcc).

items.name: Trade Marks Act, 1999 sections 29(8) and 30(1): comparative advertising using a rival's trade mark
items.one_line: You may name a competitor's registered mark to compare products only if the use is in accordance with honest practices and does not take unfair advantage of, or harm, the mark's distinctive character or reputation.

sources.title: Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (IP India): The Trade Marks Act, 1999
sources.supports: text of s.29(6)-(9) and s.30(1)

items.note: Act in force (IP India page read 2026-10-04; amendments after the page's version not checked). Rules: (1) s.29(8): 'A registered trade mark is infringed by any advertising' that '(a) takes unfair advantage of and is contrary to honest practices', (b) harms its 'distinctive character' or (c) 'is against the reputation of the trade mark'. (2) s.30(1): nothing in s.29 prevents use of a registered mark 'for the purposes of identifying goods or services as those of the proprietor' if the use 'is in accordance with honest practices' and 'is not such as to take unfair advantage of or be detrimental to the distinctive character or repute of the trade mark'. (3) s.29(9): spoken use of a word mark counts as use: a voice-over naming the rival is covered. (4) s.29(6)(d): use 'in advertising' is use of the mark. For copy: compare verifiable facts (price, specs, tested results), name the rival plainly in text rather than copying its logo, colours or tagline, never mock or denigrate; the ASCI Code adds a non-denigration rule (comp:asci_code) and FSSAI bans food ads that undermine another maker's products (comp:fssai_advertising_claims_2018). Indian courts have read these sections in many comparative-ad cases; no case law harvested here.

items.name: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Greenwashing or Misleading Environmental Claims, 2024
items.one_line: Environmental claims in Indian ads (green, eco-friendly, natural, sustainable, carbon-neutral, plastic-free, net-zero) need qualifiers, accessible verifiable evidence from independent studies or third-party certification, and full disclosure; vague, selective or imagery-only green claims are banned.

sources.title: Central Consumer Protection Authority, F. No. CCPA/28/2023-CCPA (Reg.): Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Greenwashing or Misleading Environmental Claims, 2024 (signed scan)
sources.supports: clauses 2 (definitions), 3 (application), 4 (prohibition), 5 (substantiation), 6 (disclosures), 7 (aspirational claims), Annexure 1 illustrations

sources.title: Department of Consumer Affairs 'What's new': same Guidelines PDF
sources.supports: official copy of the same signed document

items.note: Issued under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 as a furtherance of comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022 (clause 1 heading); the scanned PDF carries no notification date and the PIB release was not read, so the exact 2024 issue date is NOT confirmed here (PDF read as page images 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) generic terms 'clean', 'green', 'eco-friendly', 'good for the planet', 'minimal impact', 'cruelty-free', 'carbon-neutral', 'natural', 'organic', 'pure', sustainable, regenerative 'shall not be used without adequate, accurate and accessible qualifiers and substantiation' (cl. 5(a)). (2) 'All environmental claims shall be supported by accessible verifiable evidence based on independent studies or third-party certifications' (cl. 5(c)); specific claims (compostable, recyclable, plastic-free, climate-positive, net-zero etc.) need disclosure of the certification or evidence (cl. 6(5)); a QR code or URL can carry the detail (cl. 6(1)). (3) Say whether the claim covers the product, packaging, process, use or disposal (cl. 6(3)); Annexure illustration: 'recyclable' on a package is misleading if it is unclear whether the package or the product is recyclable. (4) Comparative green claims must 'disclose exactly what specific aspects are being compared' ('greener than the competition!' is the Annexure's misleading example) (cl. 6(4)); no cherry-picked research (cl. 6(2)). (5) Aspirational claims ('net-zero by 2030') only with 'clear and actionable plans' (cl. 7); no green imagery that implies eco-friendliness without substance, and no non-existent or unrecognised eco-seals (Annexure 1, items 5-6). Not covered: obvious puffery, generic colour schemes, and a company mission statement not tied to a product (cl. 2(f)).

items.name: X (Twitter) Paid Partnerships Policy
items.one_line: Creators posting paid, gifted, affiliate or ambassador content on X must switch on the 'Paid Partnership' content disclosure, follow local advertising law, and may not promote listed industries (health supplements, weight loss, pharma, alcohol, political or social-issue content, and more) through paid partnerships.

sources.title: X Help Center: Paid Partnerships Policy
sources.supports: definition of paid partnership, disclosure toggle, legal compliance, prohibited industries, country rules (Australia, EU, UK)

items.note: Current policy page read in a browser 2026-10-04 (python fetch got HTTP 403; page shows no date). Rules: (1) a paid partnership includes products 'gifted by or on behalf of a brand', monetary or in-kind compensation, 'a commission for you from sales, for instance, through affiliate links or discount codes', and brand-ambassador agreements. (2) Paid-partnership posts 'must have the “Paid Partnership” disclosure on', set in Content Disclosure settings when posting; X then labels the post. (3) 'You are responsible for ensuring that any Paid Partnership that you post complies with all applicable laws and regulations', and the product, service or CTA must be 'clearly promoted without requiring users to click on any additional links'. (4) Not eligible globally: adult products, alcohol, contraceptives, dating, drugs incl. CBD, 'Geo-political, political, social issues or crises for commercial purposes', health and wellness supplements, pharma and medicine, tobacco and vapes, weapons, weight-loss products; in Australia, the EU and the UK also financial products (loans, investments, crypto, BNPL) and gambling. (5) UK: own-brand posts by someone with a commercial interest also need a disclosure. For India also follow comp:asci_influencer (label in the post itself, not only the platform toggle).

items.name: Representation of the People Act, 1951 section 127A: printer and publisher on election pamphlets and posters
items.one_line: Every printed election pamphlet, hand-bill, placard or poster in India must carry the names and addresses of its printer and publisher on its face, backed by a signed, attested publisher declaration sent with a copy to the election authorities.

sources.title: Indian Kanoon (secondary reproduction of statute text): Section 127A in The Representation of the People Act, 1951
sources.supports: full text of s.127A(1)-(4)

sources.title: Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice: Representation of the People Act, 1951 (Act No. 43 of 1951)
sources.supports: official landing page for the Act (page body did not load for the fetch client on 2026-10-04)

items.note: In force (section text read on Indian Kanoon, a secondary but verbatim reproduction, 2026-10-04; the Legislative Department page returned no body to the fetch client: medium confidence on currency). Rules for poster, leaflet and print-ad copy during an election: (1) s.127A(1): no one may print or publish 'any election pamphlet or poster which does not bear on its face the names and addresses of the printer and the publisher thereof': the imprint line is part of the copy, never optional. (2) s.127A(2): the publisher gives the printer a signed identity declaration 'attested by two persons to whom he is personally known', and the printer sends a copy of it with the document to the Chief Electoral Officer (state capital) or the district magistrate. (3) s.127A(3): 'printing' is any process for multiplying copies 'other than copying it by hand', and an 'election pamphlet or poster' is any printed material 'for the purpose of promoting or prejudicing the election of a candidate', excluding mere meeting-date notices and routine instructions to workers. (4) s.127A(4): up to six months' imprisonment, or fine up to two thousand rupees, or both. The section speaks of printed documents; digital campaign ads are handled through ECI's MCMC pre-certification (comp:eci_mcc) and platform disclaimers (comp:meta_siep_ads, comp:google_election_ads).

items.name: IRDAI rules for insurance advertisements (Master Circular on Protection of Policyholders' Interests, 2024)
items.one_line: Any Indian insurance ad, including social media posts by insurers and their distribution channels, must carry the insurer's registered name and the product's unique identification number (UIN), and is only indicative: buyers must be sent to the prospectus and benefit illustration.

sources.title: IRDAI/PP&GR/CIR/MISC/117/9/2024 dated 5 Sep 2024: Master Circular on Protection of Policyholders' Interests, 2024 (copy hosted by CAalley, a third-party site)
sources.supports: 'Advertisements' section of the customer information sheets; pilot-product publicity disclosures

items.note: STATUS PARTLY CONFIRMED: the Master Circular is dated 5 Sep 2024 (read 2026-10-04 from a third-party copy because irdai.gov.in was not reachable through search or fetch in this session: medium confidence). Whether IRDAI's earlier stand-alone advertisement regulations (Insurance Advertisements and Disclosure Regulations, 2021) are still in force or were subsumed in the 2024 regulatory overhaul was NOT confirmed; read irdai.gov.in before advising an insurer. Rules found in the circular: (1) insurers and distribution channels may advertise on TV, radio, 'social media circulations', newspapers, pamphlets; the information in such ads is 'indicative and may not provide complete details of the product'. (2) 'Insurance advertisements carry the registered name of the insurers and unique identification number (UIN) of the insurance products, wherever insurance product is advertised': put both in every product post, reel caption and banner. (3) The prospect 'should read the prospectus of the product along with the customized benefit illustrations' before buying: close with a pointer to them, never with a guaranteed-return promise. (4) Pilot products: all sales and publicity material must disclose that the product is a pilot and close-ended. Influencers talking insurance must show their IRDAI licence upfront (comp:asci_influencer).

items.name: Amazon.in Seller Central restricted products policy (listing claims, national symbols, eminent personalities)
items.one_line: Amazon.in listings may not claim that a cosmetic, wellness or other product diagnoses, cures, treats or prevents disease unless a regulator approved the claim, may not list products banned from advertising under the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act, and may not sell non-media products bearing the national flag, State Emblem or eminent Indian personalities.

sources.supports: list of restricted categories incl. national flag, State Emblem, eminent personalities, OTC and homeopathic products

sources.title: Amazon Seller Central (India): Cosmetics, skin, and hair care
sources.supports: no disease claims without regulator approval; no products prohibited from advertising under the DMR Act

sources.title: Amazon Seller Central (India): Products with the name or pictorial representation of eminent Indian personalities
sources.supports: ban on non-media products bearing the PM, President, Gandhi, Nehru and others

items.note: Public help pages read in a browser 2026-10-04 (no login needed; pages carry no 'last updated' date; Amazon.com's US equivalent was not read: its python fetch returned only navigation). Rules for listing titles, bullets and A+ copy: (1) prohibited: a listing 'claiming ... the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment or prevention of disease ... unless the claim is approved by the food and drugs regulatory authorities' (Cosmetics page): write 'helps moisturise', not 'cures eczema'. (2) Prohibited: 'Products which are prohibited from being advertised under the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisement) Act, 1954' (see comp:dmr_act_1954). (3) 'All listings and products must comply with all laws and regulations.' (4) No non-media products printed with the name or picture of the Prime Minister, President, Mahatma Gandhi, Nehru, Lal Bahadur Shastri, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, Indira Gandhi and others listed, and none with 'a pictorial representation or colourable imitation' of the Indian National Flag or the State Emblem (restricted products list; mirrors comp:emblems_names_act_1950). (5) Separate restricted pages exist for OTC drugs, homeopathic products, a 'Distorted India map' and others: open the category page before writing a listing in those categories.

items.name: W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2: success criteria that govern published copy
items.one_line: The global web accessibility standard: every image needs a text alternative, videos need captions, link text must say where it goes, pages need descriptive titles and headings, the page language (and any switch of language) must be declared, and text should be readable at lower-secondary level or come with a simpler version.

sources.title: W3C Recommendation 12 December 2024: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2

items.note: Current W3C Recommendation, version dated 12 December 2024 (read 2026-10-04). A standard, not a law by itself: laws and procurement rules point to it (India's GIGW 3.0 adopts WCAG 2.1 criteria: comp:gigw_3). Copy rules: (1) SC 1.1.1 (Level A): 'All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose': write alt text that says what the image shows or does, not 'image'. (2) SC 1.2.2 (A): 'Captions are provided for all prerecorded audio content in synchronized media'; SC 1.2.4 (AA) for live audio. (3) SC 2.4.4 (A): 'The purpose of each link can be determined from the link text alone or from the link text together with its programmatically determined link context': no bare 'click here' or 'read more'. (4) SC 2.4.2 (A): 'Web pages have titles that describe topic or purpose'; SC 2.4.6 (AA): 'Headings and labels describe topic or purpose.' (5) SC 3.1.1 (A): page language 'can be programmatically determined'; SC 3.1.2 (AA): each passage in another language too (Hindi lines inside an English page, Hinglish blocks), except proper names, technical terms and words that have become vernacular. (6) SC 3.1.5 Reading Level (AAA): when text needs reading ability 'more advanced than the lower secondary education level', provide supplemental content or a simpler version. (7) SC 1.4.3 (AA): text contrast at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text), which matters for text on images and thumbnails.

items.name: Guidelines for Indian Government Websites and Apps (GIGW) 3.0
items.one_line: Government of India's standard for every ministry, department and agency website and app: quality, accessibility and security, with accessibility success criteria adopted from WCAG 2.1 (alt text, captions, link purpose, page language) and conformity certified by STQC.

sources.title: NIC / India Portal: Guidelines for Indian Government Websites and apps (GIGW 3.0), Introduction (last updated Sep 25, 2026)
sources.supports: history (2009, 2.0 in 2019, 3.0), joint formulation with STQC and CERT-In, CQW certification expectation

sources.title: GIGW 3.0: Accessibility guidelines and attributes
sources.supports: success criteria adopted from WCAG 2.1, with 'Government organisation action' for each (e.g. 5.2.1 text alternatives, 5.2.3 captions, 5.2.30 link purpose, 5.2.38-39 language)

items.note: GIGW 3.0 is current on the official portal (page 'Last Updated: Sep 25, 2026', read 2026-10-04); its release date was not shown on the pages read. Applies to government websites, portals, web apps and mobile apps, so it binds content written for ministries, PSUs and party-government publicity sites hosted by government. Rules: (1) the accessibility criteria 'have been adopted from W3C Web content accessibility guidelines' (WCAG 2.1); each one names a 'Government organisation action' (content owner) and a 'Developer action'. (2) 5.2.1: 'A meaningful explanatory text equivalent must be specified for images and other non-text content... the description ‘Picture’ ... does not serve any purpose'; decorative images get a blank alt. (3) 5.2.3: captions for all pre-recorded audio in synchronised media; 5.2.2 transcripts for audio-only. (4) 5.2.30: link purpose clear from link text or its context; 5.2.38-5.2.39: page language and changes of language programmatically identified (matters for bilingual Hindi-English pages). (5) Organisations are 'expected' to assess sites against GIGW 3.0 and 'obtain CQW certification from the STQC Directorate' (Introduction). The general standard behind it: comp:wcag_22; the statute: comp:rpwd_act_accessibility.

items.name: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016: accessibility of information, media and services (ss.40, 42, 46, 89)
items.one_line: India's disability law requires government to ensure audio, print and electronic media content is in accessible format with audio description, sign language and closed captions, and requires government and private service providers to follow the accessibility rules framed under it.
aliases: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016

sources.title: Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (linked from depwd.gov.in/en/acts): The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (No. 49 of 2016), gazette text
sources.supports: text of ss.40, 42, 46 and 89

sources.title: Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities: Acts and Rules
sources.supports: links to the Act, the RPwD Rules and the RPwD (Amendment) Rules, 2023 on accessibility standards for ICT products and services (that PDF timed out on 2026-10-04)

items.note: Act No. 49 of 2016 dated 27 Dec 2016 (gazette text read 2026-10-04). The 2023 amendment rules on ICT accessibility standards are listed on the DEPwD page but their PDF could not be downloaded, so which standard they prescribe is NOT confirmed here. Rules: (1) s.40: the Central Government frames accessibility standards for, among others, 'information and communications, including appropriate technologies and systems'. (2) s.42: the appropriate Government 'shall take measures to ensure' that 'all contents available in audio, print and electronic media are in accessible format' and that electronic media provide 'audio description, sign language interpretation and close captioning'. (3) s.46: 'service providers whether Government or private shall provide services in accordance with the rules on accessibility' framed under s.40, within two years of those rules. (4) s.89: contravening the Act or rules: fine up to ten thousand rupees for a first contravention, fifty thousand to five lakh rupees for later ones. For a writer: caption every video, write alt text and transcripts, and expect accessibility clauses in government and large-brand briefs (see comp:gigw_3, comp:wcag_22).
